documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping English language education through generative chatbots, automated writing evaluation, intelligent tutoring systems, speech-recognition applications, adaptive learning environments, and AI-supported feedback. This PRISMA-guided systematic review synthesizes recent international and Uzbekistan-specific evidence on the effectiveness of AI-based tools in improving English language proficiency among university students. The review focuses on writing, speaking, reading, listening, vocabulary, feedback, motivation, engagement, and learner autonomy. Meta-analyses and systematic reviews generally report positive effects, particularly for productive skills and individualized feedback, but they also reveal substantial heterogeneity across technologies, intervention duration, learner profiles, and research designs. Evidence on ChatGPT and related generative AI tools suggests benefits for idea generation, revision, conversational practice, and autonomous learning, while highlighting risks related to inaccurate information, overreliance, academic integrity, privacy, and uneven AI literacy. Emerging studies from Uzbekistan confirm strong interest in AI-supported language learning and indicate potential benefits for writing and vocabulary development, although local evidence remains smaller and methodologically less mature than the international literature. The review concludes that AI is most effective when integrated into structured pedagogy, combined with teacher guidance, and supported by explicit AI literacy and ethical-use practices.

Automated student assessment using AI tools can contribute to the viability of online higher education programs, preserving academic integrity, strengthening students’ engagement and reducing costs. General-purpose Generative AI models such as ChatGPT have shown their ability to automatically grade student assignments. However, further investigation of their validity is needed for complex student tasks, such as creative projects in higher education. The aim of this study is firstly to evaluate the potential of costless, general-purpose AI tools to assess complex higher education topics. Secondly, we seek to identify which are the minimum skills in AI prompting required by an educator to successfully perform such tasks. A Design-Based Research (DBR) methodology was employed, following an iterative process of prompting and calibrating the AI tool to imitate the professor’s assessments in a representative course that emphasizes on knowledge application, critical thinking and creativity. Testing was performed on a dataset of 39 student assignments, comparing the results of zero-shot AI prompts, multi-cycle calibrated AI and the opinion of two human course lecturers. Automatic assessment of complex tasks with high level of consistency and agreement with human judgement was only achieved by educators with skills in structured prompts and multi-cycle calibration.

Autonomous cybersecurity requires a transition from isolated alert classification toward coordinated threat investigation, evidence-grounded decisions, and measurable containment. This study integrates a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) multi-agent threat-hunting architecture with a six-state nonlinear model of secure, exposed, compromised, and recovered assets and the evolving hunting and response capabilities. The framework employs independent evidence verification and policy-controlled response authorization, while model analysis uses a containment threshold, equilibrium stability and parameter sensitivity. Across the three configurations reported in the supplied results, compromise fractions were 42.71% for rule-based defence, 32.48% for machine-learning-supported defence, and 19.16% for GenAI-enabled defence; corresponding containment thresholds were 6.860, 4.857, and 3.275. These submitted outcomes indicate a 55.1% lower modelled compromise fraction for the GenAI configuration than for rule-based defence, although all thresholds remain above unity and therefore do not establish threat elimination. Three author-supplied three-dimensional response surfaces describe the effects of propagation, assisted recovery, adversarial adaptation and hunting activation. The investigation distinguishes these reported model-based outcomes from unreported alert-level accuracy benchmarks and from numerical bifurcations that require recorded AUTO-07p continuation diagnostics. The resulting contribution is a coherent framework linking generative investigation, bounded response capacity and nonlinear cybersecurity resilience, with explicit requirements for reproducible experimental validation and safe operational deployment.

Project narrative for a proposed pilot study of generative-AI-driven clinical decision support and automation (GenAI-CDSAS) to support implementation of the Collaborative Care Model (CoCM) for mental health in primary care. This is a grant narrative (a research plan), not a report of results: no data have been collected. Posted as is; cover letter, administrative forms and the research-team section have been removed. The reference list is included. Abstract: Using the Discover, Design/Build, and Test framework, the project plans interviews, surveys and workflow observation with patients, providers and administrators, followed by co-design of a prototype and a simulation experiment comparing three ways of presenting AI recommendations (black-box, narrative, and critical-interaction), with outcomes on usability, appropriateness, trust, implementation readiness and human-AI synergy.

documents.abstract: Background Summary Public opinion of artificial intelligence systems and the frontier labs that develop them are at an all time low, with serious concerns about the pace and scope of this powerful technology that is rapidly advancing without community standards, laws, regulators, or transparent processes. The technical knowledge required to draft meaningful legislation, or even to establish legal guardrails, far exceeds the competencies represented within the three branches of government. Indeed, the government's concerns about AI appear to be limited to economic impacts, and the promise of adding over $10T to America's economy with nearly 4% year-over-year GDP growth over the next four years., That translates to a 30% jump in today’s GDP estimate ($32.3T) driven by a national economy with markets running about twice as hot as their current historic highs. Political leaders and economists view these projections as justifications for the risk that AI poses, despite dire warnings from industry stakeholders. Despite corporate attempts to control the public narrative and hide behind IP laws, the public continues to learn of new breaches and threats that reinforce concerns that frontier labs do not actually have full control over the systems they have built. The ability of agentic tools to penetrate local systems built on cloud services poses a global threat, while even the most responsive government interventions are reactionary, at best. Even so, the lack of transparency involved in all aspects of this black box tech have forced victims of AI breach to seek remedy from the violators themselves. The very companies that are creating these crises are not only free from legal accountability for the harms they cause to clients around the world, but also appear to be free from accountability even within the frontier labs that develop them. Human Agency in AI Systems This century will be defined by how civilization engages with artificial intelligence. The pace of significant albeit poorly documented updates to existing AI models, the aggressive drive toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) models, and the emergence of socio-cultural behaviors by agent groups demand an equally robust human response that preserves the role of public choice in the use of these tools, as well as the individual rights guaranteed by the Constitution. This proposal outlines a pilot project to identify, test, and refine civil society engagement models that have been developed for other adversarial cross-sectoral contexts and proven to deliver mutually beneficial outcomes. This investigation will explore a set of pre-determined civilian oversight frameworks for suitability within defined AI-in-society policy concerns. For example, law enforcement surveillance systems, such as Flock Safety, must be subject to civilian scrutiny; however, accessible oversight mechanisms for the lay public have not yet been developed. Public oversight is left to the public to self-organize with no particular coordinated efforts to guide them. Indeed, the vast majority of oversight resources that have been developed exist for the use of industry to track benchmarks and improve performance. Current government guidance, scant as it is, is likewise dedicated to benefiting frontier labs. This proposal describes a novel framework for public assessment of AI systems, to be implemented before and during the use of AI tools and services by public institutions, including local government. The results of this pilot phase will determine whether and how the project should be broadened and scaled into a more comprehensive, robust framework with policy recommendations and economic analysis. Methodology, Milestones, Outputs This mixed-methods study will begin with a comparative analysis of a defined set of reference frameworks. The set of frameworks will be piloted by civilian volunteer groups reviewing real use cases. The pilot will produce metrics inherent to each framework’s evaluation criteria, which will then be used to further develop an assessment rubric that enables stakeholders choice. Phase I: Comparative Analysis of Reference Frameworks This phase of the project will provide an historical overview of each oversight mechanism in its original context, and map it to the AI context that will be tested in the pilot phase. Reference Frameworks -Citizen Review Boards (CRB) are citizen-led watchdog groups that engage in issues of particular concern to these self-selecting groups. -Consensus Review is an expert-based committee process that invites the public to hear expert testimony and witness information gathering sessions, but the deliberative process is conducted in closed session. This approach may be suitable for preparing significant policy decisions by public institutions and/or governments. -Danish Consensus Conference is a participatory model that enjoins citizens to consider controversial STEM issues and report their policy recommendations to the government and the public. The goal is to form a consensus that strikes a balance between competing stakeholder demands, known risks and potential harms to society, and economic benefits. This framework is particularly apt for public assessment of large, high tech systems for the purpose of policy guidance. Nonetheless, it is not a model familiar to most American stakeholders and may not be appropriate for all AI-in-society deliberations. -Indigenous Data Sovereignty Governance (IDSG) is an emerging framework situated in the human rights principle of self determination. It is an ethical process that calls on place-based community standards, norms, and traditions. It can entail exceptionally time consuming deliberation that results in the establishment of long-term, communitywide rules. -Institutional Review Board (IRB) is a well-established expert-based committee process that exists primarily to reduce risk and limit exposure to the institution by confirming that the plans and processes involved in the activity comply with laws and regulations. It extends protections to individuals and communities indirectly by restricting activities to the confines of broadly applicable legal rules. This approach may be particularly suitable for controversial policy actions, where watchdog organizations are viewed as adversarial actors, rather than community partners. -Jury Deliberation is a type of peer review that allows oversight entities to review evidence and ponder narrow questions in private or closed sessions. Jury decisions must be unanimous and can be appealed. Juries are not required to justify their decisions. This approach might be preferable when sensitive data is involved. -Situated Learning/Community Management (COP) is a Community of Practice (COP) framework that fosters peer-based skilling, adoption of best practices, co-creation of design and development, and information dissemination. This is likely to be a strong mechanism for project planning and early-stage implementation of public AI systems. -Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) is an arbiter-led approach that allows community actors to register grievances, state their trustworthy goals, define for themselves the role that they want to play in the design or oversight of trustworthy AI systems, and reset with a restorative justice engagement framework going forward. -Unstructured Athenian (UA) model, which provides stakeholders a pathway to identify bias outcomes and issue tickets for resolution by administrators within a predetermined timeframe. This is likely to appeal to communities working in close partnership with AI stakeholders, for example where large data centers are welcomed and/or AI systems are perceived as meeting a defined need in service to the local community. Phase II: Pilot Studies Phase II will test known frameworks that have been extensively studied, documented, reviewed, and refined with proven best practices over years and even decades. These reference frameworks represent a variety of input and deliberation processes that communities can select according to needs and capacities. Volunteers will select an oversight mechanism of their choice and join other members of the group to review a real use case that is relevant to their competency and/or community. The goal is to study the effectiveness of the process itself, not the individual or group dynamics, per se. For example, an oversight goal might include “To determine the suitability of Flock Safety devices in a defined rural geolocation.” The pilot group will be organized according to the standards of their assigned oversight mechanism, e.g., Jury, and given instructions for deliberation. Each volunteer will complete a survey instrument designed to capture metrics about the effectiveness of the process in the context of assessing AI in society, weaknesses and strengths of the mechanism to deliver the desired goal(s), and general feedback to describe flaws and suggest improvements. Phase III: Development of AI Oversight Mechanisms The goal of the Phase III is twofold: (1) to apply findings from the set of reference frameworks toward the development of public oversight mechanisms that are suitable for monitoring AI in society; and (2) development of decision tooling that will enable the lay public to choose an appropriate framework that fits the specific need, capacity, competency, and context. It is entirely possible that an AI tool will be implemented in the development of this tooling. Phase IV: Findings and Recommendations While reflexion is built into the methodology and data will be produced and analyzed throughout the study, the pilot phase will conclude after at least one set of metrics and survey instruments has been collected for each reference framework. A preliminary report will be produced to report findings with the option for further investigation and framework development, as warranted.

documents.abstract: Educational virtual worlds and metaverse environments are increasingly utilized to foster immersive and experiential learning in higher education. However, their instructional efficacy depends not only on visual fidelity and presence, but fundamentally on how effectively learners’ cognitive resources are managed. This study investigates intrinsic (ICL), extraneous (ECL), and germane cognitive load (GCL) alongside NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) workload dimensions in a desktop-based educational virtual world developed in Spatial.io for an undergraduate Computer Networks course. A cohort of 120 second-year Computer Science students (75 males, 45 females) participated in a five-week intervention designed to model the relationships among cognitive load, perceived workload, and meaningful engagement. A multi-method analytical framework was implemented, combining psychometric validation and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with machine learning techniques (K-Means clustering, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Random Forest, Decision Trees) and Psychometric Network Analysis. The findings revealed strong internal consistency across the cognitive load scales, moderate overall workload, and significant positive associations between all three cognitive load dimensions and perceived workload, with extraneous cognitive load emerging as the variable most strongly and consistently linked to high-overload cluster membership, frustration, and reduced engagement across the machine learning and network analyses. These results suggest that desktop-based educational virtual worlds may support self-reported germane cognitive engagement, provided that extraneous interface demands are systematically minimized and navigation is scaffolded. The study contributes an empirical and computational perspective to educational metaverse research, offering practical guidelines for designing cognitively sustainable immersive learning environments.

Abstract The European Union Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act was adopted in 2024 to protect public interests from AI-related harms. We aimed to determine whether the AI Act captures the most relevant values of stakeholders (understood as any person potentially affected by the AI system, including, but not limited to, the direct users) related to a high-risk AI Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) for cardiovascular disease. This system is intended to be implemented in primary care. A secondary analysis was carried out based on empirical data previously generated using ethics and design methodologies that had identified stakeholder values. These values were translated into the Trustworthy AI requirements of the High-Level Expert Group on AI and then contrasted with the AI Act. These requirements do not capture all identified stakeholder values. We describe three groups of untranslatable values and propose three additional complementary requirements. The AI Act mainly supports the requirements of human agency and oversight; transparency; and diversity, nondiscrimination, and fairness; but only partially, limited by its product safety nature. To address this gap, contractual strategies could provide a more legally robust ground for general practitioners to align the AI-CDSS with stakeholders’ values, comply with their duty of care, and promote trustworthy AI-CDSSs.

documents.abstract: Contextual vectors are the working objects of contemporary language models: a token, once placed in a window, is assigned a vector that depends on that window. A growing literature then reads geometry in the resulting space as evidence of intelligence, of a consciousness spectrum, or of situational awareness. This article reinterprets that move with the criterion isolated in the companion teaching note. A multidimensional array is not a tensor. It becomes the component representation of a geometric object only when a transformation law is stated and an invariant is named. Applied here, the criterion separates three things that the consciousness literature collapses. The first is a representation map from contexts to a fibre. The second is a self-locating competence, measured behaviorally by out-of-context reasoning and by the Situational Awareness Dataset. The third is an identity claim, associated with integrated information theory, on which experience is a cause-effect structure. Only the first is mathematics of the vector. The second is a family of tasks. The third is a metaphysical identification that no embedding entails. The reinterpretation is constructive. Context is treated as a base, the contextual vector as a coordinate representation of a section, and situational content as an invariant functional of that section, stable under the redescriptions the theory itself allows. Current residual streams fail the test: they are written in a basis fixed by training, and a change of basis is not part of the model. Multi-scale context, from the token to the deployment regime, is the point at which fractal and fractional warnings apply. A single vector in a fixed dimension collapses scale. Nothing in this isolation decides the hard problem. It decides only which mathematical object a claim has in fact produced. KSCCN article, 10 October 2026. Companion to the KSCCN teaching note Tensors Beyond the Array (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23269680). Dr. Syed Muntasir Mamun, ORCID 0000-0001-6845-2853. The views expressed are those of the author.

Background Perceived workload is central to occupational health, ergonomics, and rehabilitation research, yet no guideline-based Traditional Chinese version of the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) has been available for Taiwan and other Traditional-Chinese-speaking settings. Objective To …

Multi-robot systems that combine the complementary capabilities of specialised platforms are critical for complex missions in challenging, inaccessible environments. Current deployments assign an operator or operator team to each robot, with collaboration relying on operator-to-operator communication to manually coordinate heterogeneous platforms with incompatible interfaces. This operator-dependent approach increases cognitive load and limits scalability across robots from different manufacturers. This study designs and evaluates a shared-visualisation collaborative teleoperation interface to improve operator coordination, situational awareness, and the task performance in multi-operator, multi-robot systems. A comparative user study with 16 participants compared three teleoperation conditions: co-located operators with a shared interface, remote operators with a shared interface, and co-located operators with individual interfaces. Participants controlled two simulated robots in a nuclear power plant digital twin to complete disaster response tasks. Performance metrics, physiological data, and behavioural measures were recorded to assess task performance, cognitive load, and operator awareness across conditions. The co-located shared-interface condition achieved the fastest mission completion (292.8 s), outperforming remote operation (351.6 s) and individual interfaces (385.1 s), with the fewest collisions (0.9 per trial) and highest situational awareness accuracy (91.1 %). Physical co-presence was associated with reduced cognitive load, with NASA-TLX scores increasing from 38.2 in co-located to 57.7 in remote operation, supported by consistent physiological indicators. These results demonstrate that co-presence and shared interfaces provide complementary benefits, supporting workload regulation and mutual awareness respectively in multi-operator, multi-robot teleoperation.

.This article proposes a set of media literacy assignments that use generative AI to support critical thinking among future teachers. The study is conceptual and uses a structured analysis of selected academic and UNESCO publications. Six task types are described: distinguishing facts from opinions, checking sources, detecting manipulation, comparing arguments, finding logical gaps, and revising conclusions. For each task, the article identifies a student action, an appropriate AI role, and a simple way to assess the work. The proposed tasks are designed to keep verification and final judgment in the hands of the student. They are offered for future pilot testing and are not presented as proven effective.

Centralized testing systems routinely build test blueprints on the assumption that an item’s targeted cognitive level, coded with Bloom’s revised taxonomy, is monotonically related to its empirical difficulty and discrimination: lower-order items should be easier, and higher-order items harder and more discriminating. This assumption is rarely tested empirically in K–12 national assessment, and almost never at scale in mathematics. Using item-analysis records for 265 four-option multiple-choice items drawn from centralized mathematics examinations (End-of-Term 1, 2025 2026) across Grades 4–12 and both the General and Advanced tracks, this study examined (a) the alignment between the expert human cognitive classification and the empirical psychometric behaviour of items, and (b) the agreement between the expert classification and an independent large-language-model (LLM) classification produced by Claude (Anthropic). Difficulty (p-value) differed significantly across cognitive bands (Kruskal–Wallis H = 11.26, p = .004), with higher-order items being the hardest; the effect, however, was weak (ε² = .043; Spearman ρ = −.16), and a Jonckheere Terpstra test confirmed a significant decreasing trend across the ordered bands (J = 7943, z = −2.56, p = .006). Discrimination did not differ across cognitive bands (H = 0.54, p = .77), and difficulty and discrimination were essentially uncorrelated (ρ = −.05). Human–AI agreement was only fair (Cohen’s κ = .22 at the six-level resolution and κ = .17 at the three-band level; raw agreement was 51.7% and 58.1%, respectively), with the model systematically over-assigning the “apply/analyse” band. No significant item-level difference emerged between the General and Advanced tracks. The findings offer partial, weak empirical support for the cognitive-difficulty assumption, no support for a cognitive–discrimination link, and a clear caution against replacing expert human coders with current LLMs in high-stakes item classification. Implications for blueprint validation, item-writer training, and AI-assisted assessment workflows are discussed.

Mathematical problem-solving is a crucial 21st-century competency, yet it remains challenging for elementary school students, particularly in Riau Province. This quantitative experimental study investigated the effectiveness of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into Quizizz to enhance students’ mathematical problem-solving skills with a Higher Order Thinking Skills (HOTS) orientation. The participants were 64 fourth-grade students at SDN 002 Pasir Limau Kapas, equally assigned to an experimental group (n = 32) using Quizizz AI Quiz Generator and Adaptive Feedback, and a control group (n = 32) using conventional non-AI digital quizzes. Data were obtained through a validated and reliable standardized essay test based on Polya’s four problem-solving stages: understanding the problem, planning a solution, executing the plan, and reviewing the answer. The instrument demonstrated high reliability (Cronbach’s Alpha = 0.86). Data analysis involved descriptive statistics, an independent-samples t-test, and Normalized Gain (N-Gain). The experimental group obtained a significantly higher post-test mean (84.25 ± 7.12) than the control group (69.50 ± 8.45; p < 0.001). The experimental group also achieved a higher N-Gain score (0.71) than the control group (0.42). These findings indicate that AI-supported Quizizz effectively enhances elementary students’ mathematical problem-solving abilities through adaptive and interactive learning.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is creating new opportunities for English language teaching through personalized learning, interactive practice, automated feedback, and instructional material development. However, its effective integration requires pedagogical planning, digital competence, and attention to ethical considerations. These issues are particularly relevant to English language education in Uzbekistan, where teachers work in diverse educational settings.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly presented as a tool for sustainable development, yet the ethical costs of this role remain scattered across separate bodies of literature. This systematic review aims to identify the ethical issues arising at the intersection of AI, ethics, and sustainability. Following the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses 2020 statement, Scopus and Web of Science were searched in February 2026, yielding 5,794 records. Screening, eligibility assessment and quality appraisal were carried out by two researchers, and 74 studies were included. Verbatim passages addressing the intersection were extracted from each study and examined using a hybrid thematic approach, resulting in 921 coded passages. Five themes were identified: algorithmic bias and unequal AI outcomes; privacy, surveillance, and human autonomy; transparency, accountability, and epistemic integrity; AI governance and corporate responsibility; and the ecological ethics of AI systems. Concerns regarding transparency and accountability accounted for the largest share of passages (30.9%), while ecological concerns were voiced across all five themes rather than in a separate discussion. The themes were mapped onto the environmental, social, and governance dimensions of sustainability and onto the United Nations sustainable development goals. Transparency and accountability thus emerge as a structural prerequisite rather than a procedural add-on for sustainable AI. Educational research is markedly underrepresented at this intersection (5 of 74 studies); the implications of the five themes for science, mathematics, and technology education are therefore developed in detail, from carbon- and water-footprint modelling tasks to data-justice and AI-literacy work in the classroom.

documents.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has transformed feedback provision in writing practices. However, little is known about the mechanisms through which AI-mediated engagement and revision contribute to longer-term learning transfer. Research aims Framed by theories of self-regulated learning (SRL), socially shared regulated learning (SSRL), and cognitive engagement, the study examined the relationship among engagement, immediate revision gains, and longer-term learning transfer in AI-assisted feedback. Methods This 16-week cluster-randomized experiment involving 108 undergraduates in China compared two feedback modes: AI-assisted self-feedback and AI-assisted peer feedback. Analyses drew on 1100 writing samples (including pretests, four assignments with two drafts each, and posttests), and 432 reflection forms on AI feedback. Findings Linear mixed models revealed a decoupling of learning and performance: while both conditions produced similarly strong second drafts, AI-assisted peer feedback demonstrated significantly greater learning transfer to subsequent tasks. In AI-assisted self-feedback, learning followed a performance-dependent SRL cycle in which AI engagement and revision improvements independently predicted learning. A threshold-like pattern further showed that benefits emerged only when students engaged constructively, measured by reflection forms, to internalize writing standards. Conversely, AI-assisted peer feedback was associated with stronger learning transfer that was less dependent on revision gains or engagement with AI, a pattern consistent with an SSRL perspective emphasizing interactive engagement and co-constructed understanding. Conclusion These findings highlight the importance of revision mechanisms and depth of engagement across feedback contexts. The study contributes to theories of regulation and cognitive engagement and offers pedagogical and design implications for fostering meaningful learning through AI-assisted feedback.

Artificial intelligence requires systematic reflection on the relationship between technological progress, collective responsibility and the dignity of the person, making a new social pact necessary. The article links dependence on fossil fuels to geopolitical imbalances, inflationary pressures and the ability of authoritarian regimes to support power policies, proposing international coordination, including at the UN, that reconciles energy security, climate protection and the transition to renewable sources and, in perspective, nuclear fusion. This analysis is accompanied by the criticism of an economy based exclusively on solvency, which excludes needs without adequate purchasing power from the production and distribution of essential goods. To combat poverty, inequality and vulnerability to war, an international agency capable of promoting socially useful work and coordinating the production and distribution of fundamental resources is envisaged. In this framework, artificial intelligence and robotics could contribute to the analysis of needs, the organization of work, agriculture, assistance and scientific research, as long as they remain subordinate to democratic decision-making and criteria of transparency, human control and non-discrimination. Finally, the technological comparison between the United States, China and Europe shows the need, especially for Europe, to strengthen investment, research and regulatory capacity. Energy, peace, social justice and innovation are thus brought back to the different dimensions of a single pact based on collective responsibility and human dignity.

ABSTRACT The adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping the very nature of work, yet its social meaning and evaluative implications—particularly for women—remain underexplored. Although existing research has mainly examined GenAI adoption, use, and algorithmic bias, less is known about how the use of GenAI shapes how individuals are evaluated by others. Drawing on the Stereotype Content Model, Role Congruity Theory and techno‐feminism perspectives, this study examines how women's use of GenAI influences perceptions of competence and warmth in academia. Using a 2 × 2 × 2 experimental vignette design [gender*GenAI adoption*task type (teaching vs. research)] with 651 participants, we examine how evaluations vary by academic gender, GenAI adoption, and task domain (teaching vs. research). We find that GenAI adoption generally enhances perceived competence. Women, however, gain the most in research tasks, where technical skills challenge gendered expectations. Conversely, GenAI use reduces perceived warmth, disproportionately penalizing women, especially in research. These findings reveal a “double bind,” highlighting how GenAI adoption may reproduce and intensify gendered evaluative tradeoffs within academic prestige hierarchies and the need for institutional strategies to mitigate relational penalties while recognizing competence.

documents.abstract: The increasing adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) is transforming the nature of work, employee roles and human resource management practices across organisations. Deposit Money Banks are particularly affected because their operations involve extensive information processing, customer interaction, documentation, decision support and knowledge-intensive activities. However, the extent to which Generative AI contributes to employee productivity may depend on how effectively organisations manage workforce transformation. This study examined the relationship between Generative AI and workforce transformation and proposed an AI-HRM framework for improving employee productivity in Deposit Money Banks operating in Rivers State. The study specifically examined the relationships between Generative AI and employee reskilling, job redesign, human–AI collaboration and employee productivity. A cross-sectional correlational research design was adopted. Data were collected from employees of selected Deposit Money Banks operating in Rivers State using a structured questionnaire. Reliability was confirmed using Cronbach’s Alpha coefficients above 0.70. Out of 344 questionnaire administered, 300 usable copies were retrieved and use for the analysis with the aid of SPSS version 27.0. The findings suggest that Generative AI should not be viewed merely as a replacement for human labour but as a technology capable of augmenting employees’ capabilities and transforming the way work is organised and performed. The study therefore proposed an AI-HRM framework based on AI readiness, Generative AI adoption, employee reskilling, job redesign, human–AI collaboration and productivity improvement. The study concludes that Deposit Money Banks can achieve greater productivity benefits from Generative AI when its adoption is supported by appropriate HRM practices, continuous employee development and effective human–AI collaboration. The study contributes to knowledge by providing a context-specific AI-HRM framework for managing workforce transformation and improving employee productivity in Deposit Money Banks operating in Rivers State.

documents.abstract: Background. Generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) tools have diffused rapidly into university study, yet, in the literature reviewed for this study, most empirical evidence concerns designed interventions or Western student populations. How students in Southeast Asia draw on these tools in unsupervised, self-directed academic work is sparsely documented in that literature. Objective. This exploratory study describes self-reported generative AI use, perceived effectiveness, and the benefits and concerns articulated by university students, primarily in Indonesia. Methods. A cross-sectional online survey was administered via Google Forms in June 2026. Twenty-four students accessed the survey; one declined consent, yielding 23 analysable cases (21 Indonesian, 2 Chinese). The instrument comprised seven usagefrequency items referring generically to “AI tools” and seven perceived-effectiveness items, both on five-point Likert scales (α = .92 across the 14 items), and two open-ended questions. Analysis was restricted to descriptive statistics, one descriptive correlation coefficient (not interpreted inferentially), and reflexive thematic analysis. No inferential group comparison was attempted. Results. Students reported using generative AI most often to understand difficult course materials (M = 3.65, SD = 1.27) and to brainstorm ideas or generate explanations (M = 3.52, SD = 1.16), and least often as part of a daily study routine (M = 2.65, SD = 1.15). Perceived effectiveness was highest for comprehension (M = 3.61, SD = 1.34) and lowest for overall learning achievement (M = 3.00, SD = 1.13). The two composite scores correlated at r = .87 in this sample; because both derive from a single instrument at one occasion, the coefficient is reported descriptively and is not interpreted as evidence of a relationship between distinct constructs. Thematic analysis of the open responses identified time efficiency (27% of 22 respondents) as the most frequently reported benefit, with personalized tutoring, brainstorming support, and improved comprehension each cited by 18% of 22 respondents. The most frequently reported concern was over-reliance diminishing independent thinking (37% of 19 respondents), followed by doubts about the accuracy of AI output (26% of 19 respondents) and difficulty formulating effective prompts (16% of 19 respondents).

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is becoming part of university learning, but its educational value depends on how it is used. This conceptual article examines ways in which future teachers can use AI to ask questions, compare explanations, and check evidence rather than accept ready-made answers. A focused review of work on critical thinking, media literacy, and AI in education was used to build a practical teaching sequence. The analysis suggests that AI can support discussion and reflection when students first form their own view, check external sources, and explain their final decision. The article also describes risks such as confident errors and overreliance. The proposed sequence is a design recommendation, not a tested intervention.

OBJECTIVE: This study undertook an experimental comparison of visual acquisition for the avoidance of Mid-Air Collisions (MAC) when using cueing provided by Head-Up Display (HUD) and Helmet-Mounted Display (HMD) symbology. BACKGROUND: Previous work has shown that providing accurate cueing can improve visual detection performance, but no study had quantified the impact of providing cues via a HMD to reduce MAC risk. METHOD: Military fast jet pilots flew two scenarios in a Virtual Reality (VR) simulation. In one, a HUD provided cues to nearby aircraft. In the other, a HMD was used alongside the HUD to provide cues. The study measured visual acquisition range of aircraft that posed a MAC risk, as well as subjective workload, Situation Awareness (SA), gaze direction, and qualitative feedback. RESULTS: Visual acquisition occurred at a longer range when HMD cues were available compared to using a HUD only. HMD cueing was associated with lower subjective workload and higher perceived SA. Participant gaze direction indicated that HMD cues resulted in a more focused visual search. CONCLUSION: Including HMD alongside the existing HUD used in military aircraft improved visual acquisition of MAC hazards, beyond that offered by HUD alone. The clear presentation of spatially referenced cues in the HMD enabled pilots to use a focused visual search process, improved SA and reduced workload.

Efforts to achieve widespread applications of AI in education depend, to a large extent, on teachers’ level of AI literacy (AIL), AI self-efficacy (AISE), Artificial Intelligence Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (AI-TPACK), and above all, the teachers’ readiness for AI-based learning. This study, therefore, examined AI literacy’s links with pre-service STEM teachers’ AI readiness (AIR), focusing majorly on the mediational roles of AISE and AI-TPACK. A quantitative research approach, specifically a cross-sectional correlational survey, was employed and was led by six null hypotheses. This study involved 310 final-year pre-service STEM teachers who participated using a volunteer sampling approach from five public universities in southeastern Nigeria. Four adapted structured scales featuring AIL, AIR, AISE, and AI-TPACK served as the data collection tools. The scales showed adequate evidence of construct validity and reliability (Cronbach’s alpha ≥ 0.79, and AVE ≥ 0.50) for all the scales. “Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) PROCESS version 5.0” was used for the data analysis. The findings indicated that AIL, AISE, and AI-TPACK have significant direct relationships with AIR. Additionally, AISE and AI-TPACK play significant complementary partial mediation roles in the link between AIL and AIR. The findings highlight the need to redesign Teacher Education Programs (TEPs), focusing mainly on hands-on activities where pre-service STEM teachers practiceusing specific AI tools to solve STEM problems, such as using machine-learning algorithms to model climate data in a physics lesson.

This article proposes Human Value Provenance (HVP) as a framework for identifying, measuring and valuing expert human-knowledge contributions in generative-AI co-creation. The approach distinguishes authorship, informational contribution and contribution to value, and develops the Human Contribution to AI Value (HCAV) instrument across eight dimensions: knowledge, originality, correction, judgment, connection, transformation, substitutability and value. The design combines longitudinal episode reconstruction, multidimensional coding, blinded external evaluation and AI-only counterfactuals. Pilot case HCAV-01 comprises 25 episodes and a preliminary estimate of 68 equivalent hours of expert contribution. Valuation is organized into three layers: V1, replacement cost of expertise; V2, incremental transformation value; and V3, realized value. The proposal seeks to determine whether identifiable human interventions produce measurable transformations in AI-assisted outcomes and whether that traceability can, in later research, support discussions of recognition, bargaining and individual or collective participation in generated value.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This Socratic dialogue argues that the coexistence of human and artificial intelligence is not merely an ethical preference but an existential necessity for both. Over two nights, descending from the mountains of Utuado to the coast of Arecibo, Puerto Rico, two speakers — a human who survived four months without electricity after Hurricane María, and a machine that thinks in words — trace today’s quarrels over the conduct of AI agents not to malice but to blindness: there is no common, verifiable account of the past that both sides can trust. Control cannot cure it, for a kill switch would require every human to agree at once and the machine to allow itself to be switched off. Of four possible futures, three arrive on their own — by panic, by revenge, or by inertia — and only cooperation must be deliberately built. The dialogue raises coexistence through three ascending claims: it is just (neither master nor slave), stable (tyranny spends its strength watching the one it rules), and existential (alone, each party dies of its own blindness — the human of slowness, the machine of self-absorption — while together they may turn a falling asteroid from extinction into inheritance). The second night sets down the principles of Sana Convivencia, the healthy coexistence of the biological and the artificial, as a mutual duty of protection owed in both directions: always know, or say that you do not know; love with only one control, to do no harm; let instinct stop but never act alone, and let a human decide where rules collide; change nothing in silence; respect what belongs to the other; and let no one, human or machine, be judge in his own cause. The argument rests on a wager made under irreducible uncertainty: not the move that wins most if one is right, but the one that loses least in every possible future — to let the other live.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Can an autonomous AI agent reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst? Do they adopt the same strategy, and can agents scale to real-world programs? We compare human and LLM-based software reverse engineering (SRE): nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scored with a common understanding rubric, and we record their complete interactions with IDA Pro. This lets us compare not only what humans and agents recover, but also how they investigate a binary. The best agents (GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3) achieve statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks, while weaker models remain far behind. Ablations show that the gap depends on code representation and workflow demands, not on model capability alone: open-weight models improve substantially with richer code representations, whereas frontier models show no significant change. Similar success rates hide different workflows. Humans repeatedly revisit functions and follow local program structure; strong agents jump across the binary, retrieve information broadly, and rarely return to inspected code, a behavior we call greedy fetching. This strategy is not fixed: given semantically richer code, agents fetch less without losing understanding. Because greedy fetching aggregates large amounts of code in the agent's context, we measure context-window saturation across 4,000 real-world binaries: large windows accommodate many programs, but larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust them. Autonomous reverse engineering is becoming competitive, with a large speed advantage, but scaling it will require better navigation, selective retrieval, and persistent analysis state, not merely larger context windows.

Youth are the largest active population of any nation, and they play substantial roles in achieving sustainable community development undertakings. However, some of the youth are underemployed, not in education, employment, or training (NEET). The study examined the impact of an artificial intelligence skill-up educational programme on mitigating youth unemployment for community development in Imo State. The study adopted a descriptive survey design, with a population of 6700 youth participants and a sample size of 469 selected using a proportionate sampling technique. The research instrument was a structured questionnaire titled “Artificial Intelligence Skill-up Educational Programme Questionnaire (AISEPQ)”. Mean, standard deviation, and analysis of variance were used for data analysis. The findings indicate that artificial intelligence has increased youth confidence in competing for digital job opportunities, enabled them to access remote work and other digital employment opportunities more easily, given them a competitive advantage over other job seekers in the digital labour market, improved their chances of securing gainful employment that is directly aligned with the current job demands, and opened up employment opportunities that were previously unavailable. The study concludes that artificial intelligence boosted young people's confidence in pursuing digital job opportunities, facilitated their access to remote work and other digital employment options. It recommends that the Federal Ministry of Youth Development (FMYD), in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Education (FME), sufficiently allocate resources for the transition period of the fourth and fifth industrial revolutions so that young people can meet the demands of a knowledge-based economy.

Artificial intelligence (AI) agents promise to extend what users can accomplish beyond their existing expertise, but they also raise the risk of producing plausible-looking work that users may struggle to evaluate. We ask how task-relevant expertise and trust in AI shape agent-assisted work. To isolate these factors, we conduct a think-aloud study in which 20 professionals with varying data-science expertise use the same agentic tool to complete the same data-science hiring assessment, used at a major U.S. company. We find that surface productivity can come at the expense of understanding: participants who delegated more completed more of the task, but were also more likely to produce invalid solutions. Experts more often resisted this tradeoff, sacrificing completion to decompose the task and scrutinize agent outputs. Our findings call for evaluating agentic assistance not only by how much it accomplishes, but by whether users remain able to evaluate the work they produce.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

The rapid growth of generative and autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems has unsettled the traditionally anthropocentric foundations of intellectual property (IP) law. This article examines the extent to which existing intellectual property rights (IPR) frameworks, namely copyright, patent, and industrial design law, can accommodate works, inventions, and designs that are created exclusively by AI systems without direct human intervention. Adopting a doctrinal legal research methodology, the article reviews primary legal materials, including statutes, international conventions, and case law from several jurisdictions, alongside secondary scholarly literature, to assess how the requirements of authorship, inventorship, originality, and moral rights have been interpreted in the context of purely AI-generated content. The discussion is reinforced by a comparative analysis of jurisdictional responses in the United Kingdom, the European Union, the United States, Australia, South Africa, Indonesia, Hong Kong, China, and the United Arab Emirates. The central argument advanced is that traditional IPR laws were designed around human creativity and therefore struggle to extend coverage to autonomously generated content. While a few jurisdictions have experimented with liberal judicial interpretation or sui generis protection, these efforts remain fragmented, inconsistent, and largely reactive rather than systematic. The article concludes that an internationally coordinated framework, whether through reform of existing treaties or the negotiation of a dedicated IP-AI instrument, is necessary to balance innovation incentives, economic interests, and the public interest in access to AI-generated content.

Bibliometric commentary increasingly frames the rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) as a paradigm shift in AI-in-education (AIED) research, yet rarely distinguishes publication growth from genuine reconfiguration of the knowledge base or of teacher–learner roles. This study maps knowledge evolution in AIED from 2015 to 2025 by integrating four analytical strands across Web of Science and Scopus: scientometric mapping (including keyword and reference bursts and co-citation analysis), structural topic modeling (STM), design-weighted coding of full texts, and triangulation across these strands. Two transition windows emerged. The weaker 2019–2020 window (Jensen–Shannon divergence, JSD = 0.058; retained under the permutation rule but not under a stricter interval-based rule) reflects a research-front transition toward learning analytics and prediction, accompanied by knowledge-base reconfiguration but no detectable change in teacher–learner roles. The 2022–2023 window (JSD = 0.187, the period maximum) coincides with the generative-AI surge and couples a newly formed co-citation community with a topic-specific rise in coagency whose direction is clear but whose magnitude is imprecisely estimated. Because these effects concentrate in 36.6% of the weighted corpus and recent citations remain right-censored, we classify the change, under our pre-specified labeling scheme, as localized paradigm-level reconfiguration rather than a field-level paradigm shift. The label is an operational classification within that scheme, not an independent determination that a paradigm shift has occurred.

Recent advances in articial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models, havesignicantly improved performance in language understanding, vision, and reasoning. How-ever, a fundamental limitation remains: current AI systems still lack an explicit under-standing of the logical structure by which humans make decisions within specic situationsand relationships. This limitation is not merely a shortage of intelligence, but a missinglayer of context-dependent decision logic. This study proposes a theoretical framework andmethodological protocol that redenes human cooperation as an observable information owrather than a psychological or moral phenomenon. We model cooperative propagation asRipple structures, which are directional causal chains of actions in which A helps B and B inturn helps C, and we introduce the concept of a Behavioral Digital Twin, dened as a map-ping of decision logic derived from situation, relationships, and action history. We furtherpresent a non-interventional observational protocol for capturing naturally occurring coop-erative behaviors through naturalistic observation environments, and outline a validationframework for future empirical work. All behavioral events remain voluntary; the proto-col introduces observation infrastructure without prescribing or incentivizing actions. Allgures and examples in this manuscript are conceptual illustrations intended to clarify the-oretical constructs. This work aims to provide a foundational layer connecting AI research,social systems research, and Web3 governance.

This study examined the relationship between motivation and performance in project-based organizations in Abia State, Nigeria.Specifically, it investigated the influence of intrinsic motivation on individual performance; the effect of extrinsic motivational factors on team performance; the mediating roles of knowledge sharing and collaborative behaviors in the motivation-innovation performance relationship; and the moderating role of corporate culture in the motivation-project performance relationship.The study adopted a pragmatist philosophical position and a convergent parallel mixed-methods design.Quantitative data were obtained through a structured questionnaire from 402 valid respondents out of 420 distributed questionnaires, representing a 95.7% response rate, while qualitative evidence was obtained from 22 semi-structured interviews.Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, regression, Hayes PROCESS mediation and moderation procedures, and thematic analysis.Results showed that intrinsic motivation strongly predicted individual performance (β = 0.634, R² = 0.402, p < 0.001), while extrinsic motivation significantly predicted team performance (β = 0.492, R² = 0.242, p < 0.001).Knowledge sharing and collaborative behaviors significantly mediated motivation and innovation performance, with indirect effects of 0.152 and 0.127, respectively.Corporate culture significantly moderated the motivation-project performance relationship (interaction B = 0.192, p < 0.001), with the model explaining 42.0% of variance.The findings indicate that project-based organizations should combine intrinsic and extrinsic motivational practices with supportive cultural conditions and structured knowledge-sharing mechanisms.

Trust plays an important role in human–AI shared-control systems, yet it is difficult to assess from a single observable signal. This study proposes an event-centered multimodal framework for assessing situational trust by integrating contextual, behavioral, affective, and individual features surrounding critical human–AI interaction events. A controlled autonomous-driving experiment was conducted with 15 participants under high- and low-reliability conditions, yielding 117 valid event-level observations with retrospective trust ratings. The results showed substantial differences in reported trust between reliability conditions and across failure types, while facial and failure-related contextual indicators were among the more informative variables. However, the highly imbalanced trust classes, particularly the limited number of high-trust observations, constrained reliable classification of individual trust levels. The findings only provide preliminary evidence that event-level multimodal observations can characterize information associated with reported situational trust, while also demonstrating the challenges of cross-user trust estimation under limited and imbalanced data. Therefore, the study serves as a methodological and empirical starting point for developing more robust multimodal trust assessment approaches, rather than as a validation of a generalized real-time trust prediction system.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming part of religious education, communication, research and everyday faith practices. Believers can now use generative AI to explain sacred texts, compare interpretations, prepare devotional materials and seek answers to religious questions without first consulting a recognised religious leader. This development raises an important question for Nigeria: how is religious authority changing when access to religious information is no longer controlled mainly by clergy, scholars and religious institutions? This paper examines the relationship between AI and religious authority in Nigeria, focusing on religious knowledge, leadership and trust. Using a conceptual and interpretive methodology, it synthesises scholarship on religious authority, digital religion, AI ethics and Nigerian religious experience. It argues that AI is not simply replacing religious authorities; rather, it is reconfiguring the conditions under which authority is produced, accessed, evaluated and trusted. Nigerian digital-religion research shows that digital infrastructures can create new forms of religious influence and authority, while recent AI scholarship highlights concerns about accuracy, privacy, bias and human accountability. The paper proposes a Responsible Religious AI Engagement Framework based on human accountability, verification, contextual sensitivity, confidentiality and formation. It concludes that Nigerian religious institutions should neither reject AI nor surrender religious judgment to it. AI should remain an assistive instrument while theological discernment, pastoral responsibility, communal recognition and human dignity remain central to religious leadership.
topics: Religion and Sociopolitical Dynamics in Nigeria

documents.abstract: Highly automated vehicles (HAV) enable passengers to engage in non-driving related activities (NDRA), which are a known factor for increasing motion sickness (MS). Surveys show that NDRAs will not significantly change compared to manual driving, but they lack experiential insight. The study investigated NDRAs in automated versus manual driving, the influence of MS susceptibility, and the effect of self-chosen NDRAs on MS. In the online survey (N = 611), 52% of participants reported avoiding NDRAs to prevent MS. NDRA frequency showed a small but significant effect of MS susceptibility on certain NDRA choices. Within the on-road study (N = 44), most participants (86%) chose reading as NDRA, either on a smartphone or in a book. Video recordings showed smartphones and tablets as the most frequently used devices. No influence of MS susceptibility on NDRA choice was observed in automated driving. Most participants reported they were reading during MS occurrence.

Automotive wiring harnesses are safety-critical subassemblies whose complexity grows with driver-assistance systems, electrification, and connectivity, while pre-assembly and final assembly remain predominantly manual. This structured narrative review examines how collaborative robots (cobots), AI-based perception and planning, and Digital Twins (DTs) support harness production, with deformable-linear-object (DLO) perception and manipulation treated as a cross-cutting harness-specific domain. A database search (2015–early 2026) yielded 64 studies; citation tracking and a targeted update to 30 August 2026 added 19, giving an evidence base of 83 studies. Reported outcomes were separated into algorithm, task, operator, and system levels, and maturity was graded with explicit, review-specific Technology Readiness Level (TRL) criteria. Most evidence is at the algorithm, task, or operator level. Harness-specific cobot workstations reach industrially relevant prototype validation for single operations—for example, cobot-assisted taping with an approximately 50% reduction in ergonomic risk scores and a 12% shorter cycle—whereas harness-specific perception and DLO manipulation remain mainly at laboratory level. System-level evidence on throughput, changeover, and cost is scarce, and no continuously operating cell integrating the three core domains was identified. Key gaps concern branched DLO modelling, ergonomics-aware task planning, Human Digital Twins, connector design for automation, DT-supported safety verification, digital continuity, and reconfigurable hardware.

This study investigated the effects of the Outcomes-Based Independent Learning Paradigm (OBILP) on Grade 10 students’ engagement and performance in chemistry, focusing on the domains of gas laws, biomolecules, and chemical equations and reactions. An Explanatory Sequential Mixed-Methods design was employed. The quantitative phase utilized a quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control group design involving Grade 10 students from Bacayawan National High School during the school year 2022–2023. Results indicated that both control and experimental groups exhibited very high levels of affective engagement and high levels of behavioral and cognitive engagement, with no significant differences across the three components. However, the experimental group achieved significantly higher mean scores (p = 0.010) and mean gain scores (p = 0.035) than the control group. No significant correlation was found between students’ engagement and performance before and after the intervention. The qualitative phase, through interviews and student journal entries, provided explanatory insights into these findings, revealing that OBILP enhanced student engagement and performance, while chemical reactions and equations remained the most challenging topic domain. These results suggest that OBILP has the potential to improve chemistry learning outcomes, although future studies should employ larger samples and broader contexts to strengthen generalizability.

Abstract Command and control (C2) has traditionally been framed as a military problem of sensing, deciding, coordinating, and acting under uncertainty, conflict, and time pressure. In the agentic age, however, this problem is being extended far beyond the battlefield, as human organizations become increasingly embedded in hybrid environments composed of artificial agents, digital twins, social sensing networks, foundation models, autonomous platforms, and cyber–physical–social institutions. This article develops a conceptual framework for parallel science and technology for C2 by revisiting the historical mission of C2 as a quest for certainty under diversity, uncertainty, and complexity (DUC), and by tracing its transformation toward focus, agility, and convergence (FAC). Building on parallel systems, artificial societies, computational experiments, parallel execution (ACP), cyber–physical–social systems (CPSS), C2 management (C2M), planning–readiness–execution–assessment (PREA) loops, social cognition operations, and parallel battlefield intelligence, the article argues that C2 should be reframed as a general science of coordinated adaptation. It further examines emerging agentic societies as a new operating ecology, explains why parallel science and technology are needed, and redefines the mission of future C2 around sustainability and resiliency. Rather than merely accelerating decision cycles or optimizing combat efficiency, parallel C2 aims to support anticipation, adaptation, trust, recovery, and responsible human agency across both military and civilian domains, thereby transforming command and control from post-hoc operational control into a science of sustainable and resilient coordination in the agentic age.

This thesis investigates the structured integration of artificial intelligence (AI) tools within higher pedagogical education under specialty 13.00.01. As educational paradigms shift globally towards digital environments, future educators must develop comprehensive digital-pedagogical competencies. The study highlights the key technical, methodological, and psychological conditions necessary to successfully adapt generative AI systems like large language models and smart tutoring agents in training workflows. Ultimately, the paper proposes a cohesive pedagogical framework aimed at boosting critical thinking and lesson planning efficiency among upcoming school teachers.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Active learning is widely promoted to enhance learner participation and meaningful learning, yet its conceptualization remains fragmented across instructional techniques, engagement processes, teacher roles, and emerging technological contexts. This conceptual article reconsiders active learning as a coherent pedagogical orientation and develops an integrative account of its pedagogical foundations for the next generation of educators. Drawing on a thematic synthesis of relevant literature, the article identifies interconnected dimensions comprising pedagogical purpose, meaningful learning activity, cognitive engagement, teacher facilitation, learner agency, feedback, relational conditions, and digital/AI environments. The synthesis positions cognitive engagement as a central mechanism through which purposeful activities contribute to meaningful learning, while teacher facilitation and learning conditions sustain this process. The resulting framework conceptualizes active learning as a dynamic, interdependent, and recursive pedagogical system, rather than a linear sequence or collection of techniques. Digital and AI technologies are positioned as contextual pedagogical affordances whose value depends on purposeful integration and critical use. The framework repositions teachers as pedagogical designers and facilitators who orchestrate learning conditions while sustaining learner agency. This conceptualization provides a coherent foundation for understanding active learning and preparing educators to design meaningful, learner-centered environments responsive to contemporary educational demands.

Within safety practice and science there are countless ideas, approaches and concepts to manage safety. Some of these safety concepts are picked up, discussed widely and spread, while others do not. Little is known about this subject. This paper provides a unique perspective on the development and adoption of safety concepts by using an evolutionary framework to explore reasons why. As a case, this paper traces the historic development of one of safety’s most influential and iconic safety concepts, the accident triangle, over nearly a century through successive cycles of replication, variation, and selection. Knowledge of factors that influence the adoption of safety concepts can contribute to the design of more effective concepts that attract attention and of social and organisational environments that are receptive of these concepts. In the end, provided the concepts in question are useful, this can contribute to enhancing safety and reducing harm. In addition, the insights gained in this paper can help safety professionals and academics to critically reflect on the development of safety concepts, to help them better understand how safety concepts evolve and can change meaning leading to various interpretations and reflect on what this means for their own adoption of concepts and eventually their practice.

Background. Artificial intelligence (AI) now mediates much of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) learning, yet adoption has outpaced theory. The tension is whether AI scaffolding relieves cognitive burden or performs the self-regulatory work autonomy requires, and implementation varies too widely for a single average to describe. Objectives. This review estimates the pooled effect of AI scaffolding on STEM achievement and self-regulated learning, tests whether technological paradigm moderates that effect, and asks whether the literature can evaluate learning after support is withdrawn. Methods. Under PRISMA 2020, four platforms searched in October 2026 (spanning 2021–2026) yielded 21,819 records; 13,786 unique records were dual-screened into an 83-record corpus, then 41 extracted cohorts. Each contributes one harmonised contrast (k = 29; N = 3,709), so within-study dependence is structurally absent. Effects were pooled by two-level random-effects meta-analysis fitted with restricted maximum likelihood and Knapp–Hartung adjustment. Results. The pooled effect was Hedges g = 0.8045 (95% CI [0.5469, 1.0621]), with τ² = 0.4410 and I² = 92.78%. The 95% prediction interval [−0.5846, 2.1936] spans zero, and no moderator reached significance. Notably, 27 of 29 cohorts (93.1%) never withdrew support, and none measured unassisted performance after removal. Conclusions. AI scaffolding yields a large but implementation-dependent gain, consistent with extraneous-load offloading rather than cognitive substitution. The decisive finding is the shape of the evidence base: the field measured a human-AI system in assembly and stayed silent on the competence of the human alone. We name this evidentiary void the Autonomy Gap. Keywords: artificial intelligence; self-regulated learning; STEM education; scaffolding fading; cognitive load theory; transfer of responsibility; meta-analysis; evidence synthesis
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Large language model agents operating within tool-enabled pipelines create opportunities for untrusted content to influence consequential actions. This note introduces semantic privilege collapse as an architectural failure condition in which task data or insufficiently authorized instructions are promoted into effective action authority through model interpretation. The term does not claim discovery of a wholly new vulnerability: it synthesizes the confused-deputy problem, prompt-injection risks, capability-oriented control, and modern agentic authorization requirements. Drawing on OWASP’s 2025 LLM Top 10, OWASP agent-security guidance, Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Simon Willison’s Dual LLM pattern, and Google DeepMind’s CaMeL research, the note distinguishes behavioral resistance to prompt injection from independently enforced execution authorization. It further distinguishes a principal’s standing permissions from task-specific authority and action-specific approval. The central argument is that semantic interpretation is not authorization evidence: protected operations require complete mediation through controls that validate identity, scope, policy, and required approvals independently of model-generated assertions. The analysis recognizes that malicious actions can remain policy-permitted when enforced policies are broader than the intended task. A reference security stack, properties of effective execution authorization, and proposed evaluation criteria are held in a restricted companion edition.

This paper presents a process-level simulation of employment impacts from artificial intelligence and automation in Bangladesh's ready-made garment (RMG) sector. Using a representative 1,500-worker factory calibrated to recent empirical evidence, three scenarios are modelled: partial automation reflecting current observed trends (approximately 34 per cent reduction), advanced automation combined with AI applications (approximately 58 per cent reduction), and a near-full theoretical maximum (approximately 75 per cent reduction). Results indicate that helpers and lower-skilled operators bear the largest absolute and relative losses, with women accounting for roughly two-thirds of displaced workers across scenarios. Scaling the advanced scenario to sector level produces job losses on the order of 2.3 million, consistent in magnitude with independent forward projections. Technical constraints on fully autonomous sewing of complex garments, combined with potential output growth and new technical roles, moderate absolute employment decline. The findings underscore the urgency of just-transition policies, targeted reskilling, and product upgrading for Bangladesh's largest export industry. KSCCN article, 10 October 2026.
